description: Portions added without mixing stay as layers; mixing merges them by a fraction per action; diffusion slowly merges them over time. Aspiration draws from the top layers.
A container's temperature approaches its place's temperature exponentially, with a time constant set by the place and scaled by volume.

A headspace is air unless purged with an inert gas through a septum; open, it is air again within minutes. Dissolved oxygen (where a liquid tracks it) tends to Henry's-law saturation with the headspace oxygen: slowly when still (kLa at 10 mL, scaled as V^-1/3), part-way at each mixing or pour, and away when the gas is bubbled through it. An unflushed syringe carries its dead space of air.

references: Air-saturated water: 8.26 mg/L O2 at 25 °C, 14.6 mg/L at 0 °C (Henry constant 1.23 mM/atm; van 't Hoff 1860 K)

description: Activity (proteins) or amount (labile reagents) decays first order, with half-lives interpolated in temperature (Arrhenius in 1/T between the declared points).

A = Σ εᵢ(λ)·cᵢ·l plus the vessel's own absorbance, observed through stray light (A_obs = −log10((10^−A + s)/(1 + s))), with additive and proportional noise, the instrument's readability and an over-range display.
Load minus tare, with repeatability noise, rounded to the balance's readability.

A liquid conducts by its ions: κ = Σ λᵢcᵢ over the charged species of the ionic equilibrium, each limiting molar conductivity lowered as exp(−0.7|z|√I/(1+√I)). Weak electrolytes conduct only through the ions they form. Unlisted ions take 55 S cm² mol⁻¹ per charge; spectator ions inside an acid–base system 60.

references: Limiting ionic conductivities at 25 °C: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics; Robinson and Stokes, Electrolyte Solutions
